A corresponding set of m real eigenvalues and linearly independent eigenvectors, understood as paired spectral data; the source does not introduce indexed notation for these pairs (printed page 3, opening paragraph, hyperbolicity definition and selected sentence).

hypotheses: The system is q_t + A q_x = 0, homogeneous, linear, and constant-coefficient in one space dimension (printed page 1, equation (1.1) and its introduction).
A has real eigenvalues and a corresponding set of m linearly independent eigenvectors, making the system hyperbolic in the stated sense (printed page 3, opening paragraph).
conclusions: Every vector in R^m has a unique expansion as a linear combination of the chosen eigenvectors (printed page 3, opening paragraph, 'uniquely decomposed').

This eigenvector decomposition provides a decomposition into component waves, with the detailed development referred to Chapter 3 (printed page 3, opening paragraph, 'this provides the decomposition into distinct waves').
Each such component wave propagates at the speed given by its corresponding eigenvalue of A (printed page 3, selected sentence).
For the illustrative acoustics matrix (1.6), the eigenvalues −c and +c are the two acoustic wave speeds (printed page 3, sentence immediately following the selected claim).
definitions_and_conventions: The subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives with respect to time and space (printed page 1, paragraph following (1.1)).
Hyperbolicity here requires real eigenvalues together with a complete independent eigenvector set (printed page 3, opening paragraph).
Wave speed is signed: the preceding acoustic example calls −c a propagation speed and associates it with motion to the left (printed page 2, final paragraph).
The scalar model explains propagation as q̃(x − ū t), preserving the profile's shape while translating it (printed page 1, equation (1.3) and following paragraph).
In the acoustic illustration, q consists of p and u, A = [[0,K],[1/ρ,0]], and c = √(K/ρ) (printed page 2, equation (1.6) and subsequent definition of c).
implicit_context: The general assertion extends the preceding separation of the acoustic system into two scalar propagation equations (printed page 2, displays for w¹ and w²; printed page 3, opening two sentences).

The selected passage is introductory prose rather than a separately numbered theorem; it announces the general wave decomposition and refers to Chapter 3 for its development (printed page 3, opening paragraph).

Interpreting the general component waves as scalar characteristic quantities is supported by the acoustic example, but the selected paragraph itself supplies no general characteristic-variable formula (printed page 2, displays for w¹ and w²; printed page 3, selected paragraph).

details: The correspondence concerns the constant real matrix in (1.1), under the full hyperbolicity condition (printed pages 1 and 3, equation (1.1) and opening paragraph).
Pairwise distinct eigenvalues are not required by the stated definition; the explicit independence requirement concerns eigenvectors (printed page 3, 'm linearly independent eigenvectors').

Unique coefficients are asserted for expansion relative to the corresponding eigenvectors; uniqueness of the choice of eigenvector basis is not asserted (printed page 3, 'linear combination of these eigenvectors').

The speed correspondence applies to the component waves obtained from that decomposition, rather than assigning a single speed to an arbitrary superposition (printed page 3, 'decomposition into distinct waves' and 'each wave').
The eigenvalue specifies signed propagation along the spatial coordinate, as confirmed by the acoustic speeds −c and +c (printed pages 2–3, acoustic propagation discussion).

An analyst can express the anticipated scalar model using a component equation w_t + λw_x = 0 and profile w̃(x − λt), but neither general formula appears in the selected paragraph; the supplied pages give scalar and acoustic instances (printed page 1, (1.2)–(1.3); printed page 2, equations for w¹ and w²; printed page 3, selected sentence).

undebatable_constraints: Retain the homogeneous constant-coefficient real system q_t + A q_x = 0 as the setting (printed page 1, equation (1.1) and following paragraph).
Retain both real eigenvalues and a complete independent eigenvector set; reality alone is not the stated hypothesis (printed page 3, hyperbolicity definition).

Associate each component wave with its corresponding eigenvalue, preserving the eigenvalue's sign (printed page 3, selected sentence and acoustic illustration; printed page 2, leftward propagation at −c).
Do not infer pairwise distinct eigenvalues from the phrase 'distinct waves'; the stated spectral requirement is independence of m eigenvectors (printed page 3, opening paragraph).
Preserve the distinction between unique expansion in a chosen eigenvector basis and uniqueness of the basis itself (printed page 3, 'these eigenvectors').

Do not present a general characteristic-variable formula or a solution regularity class as explicitly stated in the selected passage (printed page 3, opening paragraph, which announces the correspondence and refers to Chapter 3).

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional homogeneous constant-coefficient real system q_t + A q_x = 0 introduced in (1.1) on printed page 1, assume A has real eigenvalues and m corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors, as required by the hyperbolicity definition on printed page 3. Every vector has a unique expansion in that chosen eigenvector basis. The opening paragraph on printed page 3 states that this yields component waves, each propagating at the signed speed equal to its corresponding eigenvalue. The acoustic example gives speeds −c and +c. The paragraph refers the general decomposition to Chapter 3 and does not itself specify general component formulas or analytic regularity assumptions.
